blocks.x: In which part of the city?
I didn't know where I could find out. Yeah? How? Huh? How could she find out? Yeah, older men like me, you know?
He lives around here. He lives around here. I never really live around here. Oh, yeah? What's his name? Huh? What's his name, this older guy?

Well, I don't know his name, but it's a lot of old fellas. I talked to the old man the other day, he was 83. I asked him if he didn't know my dad, he said, yeah, he'd know him. He didn't know a lot of the old people. My daughter-in-law's grandmother died at the burial of Sunday. She was 93. My brother-in-law is 90. My sister is 85, 87 right now. I could ask her, maybe she might know.
Well, what's today's date anyway, family? Today? Today should be the 13th. September the 13th, 1972. That's right. Yeah.
Okay. 206 North Lopez. 706.
Yeah.
Okay, I want to get that address. Okay. Go ahead, ask some questions.
I'm writing.
Did you know Fred Washington? Fred Washington?
Yeah.
Yeah. There's a piano player.
Yeah.
Fred Washington? Good. Yeah. I know him pretty good.

Yeah. Now you want to know the fellas that I played with? Yeah. Well, I played with Chris Kelly. Played banjo. Who else was in Chris Kelly's band? Who else was in Chris Kelly's band? Who else was in Chris Kelly's band? Well, I don't know the boys. How many pieces do you have? We had five pieces. Five pieces. Five pieces. No, I played with Peek-H攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻攻 together a long time. Fats Pichon, Walter Pichon is his name. I played with him. Chris Kear, Kid Rainier, I played with him. Kid Howard, I played with him. I played with so many fellas that I forgot. We used to play together. Kid Thomas, that's Cornbread. When I played with him, we had a little band together.
That was real interesting what you were saying about Gayno.

Gayno never had a band. I was the one who knew Gayno how to play in a band. He played after me because I was probably playing this, Johnny Sensei was the first guy who showed me how to play the guitar. And then I switched from guitar to banjo. Johnny Sensei used to play with us too on the Airline Highway. In the 4900, he was on the Airline Highway. We played there. He had a little trumpet called Caledon. He said, I'll be there when you're going to get there. I said, okay. I had playing with him. I had Lawrence's dad, you know. Lawrence Tucker. Yeah, I know that. I wanted to go to the Wake, but I didn't know. And Lawrence Tucker. I had Peter William. You know Peter William, man? Peter Rabbit. Peter Rabbit, yeah. Peter Rabbit, yeah. That's how they call him. That's how the millionaire man out of Texas used to go. He was playing at the Petroleum Club. Yeah. And what's this guy that's named? I used to play with him too. I used to play around by the Hollywood. That guy that's named, he died too.
What did he play? He played Coney. You mean the guy that was any kind of Blue? No, it wasn't a kind of Blue. No, it wasn't no kind of Blue.
I played with Blue. We had a little band with Blue. Blue was playing with me. He died, boy boy. He drank so much wine, boy boy. He passed away.
Where was this place that you were playing on, Allen, Iowa? What's the name of that?
It was a nightclub. I forgot the name of that place too.
Where was the Oasis? The Oasis?

I played Frank Quintello. He was a Spanishman. Two Losing Decay. We played there. I played there about two years. I was playing piano. I played piano there. I was playing from nine to three every night.
What kind of band was it? I mean... Dixieland.

Yeah, and who else? I had Albert Francis playing drum. You know Albert. He used to play with Bruce Armstrong. And I had a fellow by the name of Hughes. He's playing the saxophone. What is his name? Hughes? Hughes. He was in the saxophone. Wallingford Hughes. Frenchie Hughes? I don't know what's his last name. I know his name was Hughes.
And... I have no copy of the family album. Who else? He's in the family album.

He's so many fellas out of the play, but... I can't think of all that damn. But... Alphonse Pico and Peter Williams. I played for Peter Williams too. Well, that was our violinist. Peter Williams was the lead man.
I wanted to ask you more about that recording session with Kid Thomas.
Well...
You know when you went over there with George? You went with George? Yeah.
I went with George, but I forgot. I know George was playing and Kid Thomas was playing, but I don't know where the rest of him was.
Well, you went. I went with him, yeah. Yeah. And he had my banjo. He didn't know about my banjo. And he never did have one.

He was nothing. My annoyance. Every time he wanted one, he'd come to me. He said, Man, let me get your banjo. I said, Okay, George. When I had two, three of them banjos, I just got rid of one. I sold.
I always had two banjos. You know what I mean? I've been having that for about four years. But what kind of... Well, you say he borrowed one once and went to Jackson, huh?
Went to Jackson, yeah. And never did give it back to him. Never did.
Well, did he hock them or what? I don't know what he'd done to him. No, he didn't hock them.

Now, he's got a banjo in the museum right now. His wife thinks that's his banjo. That wasn't his. That's his friend of mine's banjo. He borrowed it. You see, when I got to playing regular, I had a band. I made a band of my own. Me, who I had, Henry Ravallon. I had Clarence, and I got some guy's name, played the same beef right tenor. Christophe. Yeah, Harold Christophe. Harold Christophe. And I was playing the banjo. And who was somebody else again? And then after that, I got this guy to play with me. When Lawrence was playing one time, Lawrence told me, when he got sick, he couldn't play no more. And I got blue. Blue died. I had to get somebody else. So I got Leroy. You know Leroy? Leroy Thompson? They called him Leroy Thompson? Yeah, Leroy Thompson. I got him to play with me. He was playing with me from the last. And he sings and he plays. That's how I was out there.
What kind of banjo did you have when you first started?

I had a practice. A fellow by the name of Wallace. Wallace gave me that banjo. A five string banjo. And I started to play it and I bought me a book. And I started to play in it. And the fellow knocked on my door and said, Hey man, I need a banjo player for tonight. I said, I don't play no banjo. He said, Oh yeah, you do. I said, I don't. So, he said, Let me see that banjo you got. I said, I showed it to him. He said, Man, come on and play. Make this little change. So, after I played him, I went to World Islands and I bought me a banjo from the Sporey's. You know, the Sporey's. I bought a banjo from him. I bought it and played $35 worth. A little wonder. And I began to play it and play it and play it. You know what I mean? I kept on playing until I got me one. Man, I bought so many banjos and sold them, you know. I went to a doctor, a friend of mine. He's a doctor. I said, Listen, I got a nice banjo I'd like to sell you. He said, Let me see it. I said, I got it here right now. I showed it to him. He said, How much do you want for it? I said, That's why not. I said, Wrap it up. He said, Give it to me. He said, That's why not. He told me, Wherever you, you know, get a banjo, save it from me. I'll buy it from you. I said, Okay. And that time I had three banjos. So, I sold him that one. I was always on the market of buying one. You know, I bought this banjo. I was on the street. I said, Shaw Street, somewhere. I'm not wearing it. But I've not been here in about 40 years. Well, you took me a little stroll, eh? Yeah, I think I'll get out of here. Okay, see you later. There's a lot of other fellas that I played with. I just forgot who they are.
They said you played with Johnny Sincere, but he played, you mean in the same band?

Yeah, in the same band. I had a plan with it on the Airline Highway. It was all by the name of Joe, who was in the nightclub. In the 49, I'll never forget. On the 4900 Airline Highway. He used to go down there every Friday and Saturday.
Did you have two guitars? Oh no, I was playing piano. I played piano on that job. And John Sincere guitar. John Sincere guitar. And who else?

On the New Year's Eve, Lawrence told a man, everywhere we play on the New Year's Eve, the band, boss man always gives you some people whiskey. He was so small, I hit you across the head. You see, there was a little bit of guy. The guy who was playing for this big. Big like you. Big like you. Big like you. And uh...
How old were you when you played with John Sincere? Oh, that's a little bit of 20 years ago.

20 years ago? Oh yeah. Because we were playing out there. I'm playing now. 20 years. I'm on pension 20 years now. I'm on pension. I'm on my veteran pension in Social Security. See, I stopped waking when I was 62 years old. And I began to get my pension from the veteran. He was given me 6 to 15. And when I got 65, I got to get my pension. I got my Social Security and my veteran pension.
How did you play a five string banjo? Well, I was going from the book.

Did you play with fingers or with your pick? I played with the pick. I had a rap. How did you tune that fifth string? Well, I learned how to tune it. But you didn't have to tune it. I took that fifth string off. Oh, I see. I took it off. You know they got their four string, five string banjos. Yeah. Because we were rehearsing by... I had a little jam session by... What's that boy? That saxophone player that died? John. Hanging? John, Hanging's grubber, you know? Yeah. Yeah. You called them cash or something. Jewels. Jewels handy. Yeah. And we were there and the fellow had a four string, five string banjo. You know he had a four string, but it was a five string banjo. He must have took the string off, you know?
Yeah, I see. He took that... The one off that's not fretted. Yeah, yeah. The one that's not fretted.

You just play the same note? Yeah. I got a friend of mine who plays the live part of one right now. A five string banjo. He's a guitar player too. He's from here? Yeah, he's a boy from here. He'll play at the... He'll play at the... at the Preservation Hall. He's a good guitar player. He's a guitar player like Sam. A good guitar player and a good banjo player. What's his name? I just forgot him. I ain't seen him in so long. Yeah. I forgot him. And he has a five string banjo? He's got a five string banjo. I met him at the hospital when I was getting my eyes treated. Not Sunday. He's a bright looking boy. God, he's dead. I got a five string banjo player. I'm playing my body. I'm still playing my guitar too, you know? I say, yeah, okay. And who else? I even give Bill Russell a demonstration about General Roll movement. Because I went there to buy some strings, you know? And he said, by the way, he said, you know General Roll? I said, do I know him? I said, I hope I do know him. I said, I used to be with him every Monday. Every Monday. Every Monday, we cook a bean dinner for him. And, you know, serve him the dinner. And he'd be playing the piano. I said, I thought, man, I should have liked to know how to play piano. I wasn't playing. And then, you know? So, they bought the club, bought a piano. I was trying to put it upstairs and threw a rope. Put it up there. And I began to practice. I said, man, why don't you get off that piano? I said, man, I'm paying my dues here. I said, I'm supposed to play this piano all day long if I want. So, I began to practice on the piano, practice and practice until I learned how to play. I was playing. I was playing. We played at the—George and I played at the Banner Club for a long time. The man went to give us 90 hours a week and collect the tips. George said, no, indeed. We were ready to tips. Give us our little change which you give us a week and we'll collect the tips. Boy, I was making something at the Banner Club on Dolph Head Street in the 500 block right next door to where Burnell was playing. You know Burnell, huh? Yeah. Piano player boy now? Heard of him. You heard of him. You never heard of him play? No. Boy, he was a piano player. He was a piano player. I classed him as the best piano player in the state of Louisiana. Fingers like lightning. Good, good. God, the man never really knew. Fingers just like lightning. He was playing right next door to us. I don't know that man's name. Well, you know Sam Hopkins? Uh-huh. Well, that's my piano player now. Sam. But we don't—you know, people didn't kind of read all the piano. I don't know. Yeah. And whenever I get a job playing piano, we got a job we've been playing over the river for the last past seven years with some school teachers, you know? Every year. I got to call that lady up to find out if she wanted to see a condition. But Sam, he can't play. He's working. He works at the IA News. He can't play. In the daytime. There's just a day—a morning job.
Yeah, I see. Come on. Do you have his address or phone number, Sam Hopkins? Do you have Sam Hopkins' phone number or address?

Yeah, sure. I got his phone number, his address. I'll give it to you before you go. Okay, yeah. I got them all in my book. Yeah. I got them all, man. All the musicians, you know a lot of them. I got them all in my book. I had Lawrence's. You know Lawrence the piano player? Lawrence, yeah. You know Lawrence, yeah? The piano player? Yeah. I got his number, too. I had him. Because he played with me a couple of times at the pool of invocation across the river.

Those school teachers, you know? I don't know Lawrence. You know Lawrence? Well, not by his first name. He lived on Charter Street. Oh, Lawrence. Lawrence, you know Lawrence played the piano? Yeah, from Sweden. Yeah. Lawrence Edder. What's his right last name? Well, I can't pronounce it, but it's Eddergren. Eddergren.
Eddergren. Yeah. And in the Japanese, I know you know his name. The Japanese? Call him Claiborne. Yeah. Call him Claiborne.
Yeah. You're Shiotoyama and Kaikotoyama. Yeah.

Well, he gave me his name as Claiborne. Yeah, I know, but that's the book. The whole number is written 924 All-Inst Street. Yeah. Whenever I wanted him, I called him. 924. Yeah. I called him. He's coming back. He's coming back. Yeah. But I'd have to get rid of that drum player. You know?
Oh, that's right. You couldn't stand your drum, huh?

Good stand my drum. I don't know why. He played nice drums to me. Beat him up good, you know? Good a lot. He's got a drummer. He's got a drummer by Dead Big. I've never seen a beat drum right there in my life. He's one of them old time drums. Old, old drums. What's his name? His name is Paul Antoine. He's got a brother that plays guitar. You know his brother. Paul Antoine, yeah. He's got another brother that plays drums. I don't know his name. He played with me a couple of times. He waits for Undertaker people.
Yeah, he's the one that I know the best. His name is Harold. Harold Antoine, yeah. I've seen everyone in a very long time.

Well, he played with me a couple of times because Paul couldn't play in the daytime with me. All our boys, see like Harold, well Harold would play any time. Harold, not a well guard but he could play. And Sammy Hopkins, well he can't play any day. We had a lot of picnics. We played on, you know, on Sundays, Sunday evenings around, say one o'clock, twelve o'clock in the day. We played in picnics, you know. But he couldn't play them jobs.
Talking about picnics. Did you ever play on fish fries and so on? Oh, that's, I'm talking about twenty years ago. In the early days, Mark.

Yeah, twenty years ago, the back alley fish fries. Back alley fish fries. Piano in the backyard. Did you play for yourself or? No, I just played the piano myself. You know, the honk-ton. What kind of numbers did you play? Well, we played mostly blues, you know, whatever I knew. I was playing good piano one time, you know. Because I was playing with Pico, and I was playing with Albert Francis, and then I was playing piano. I played two years and I must have played passable anyhow.
Could you tell me something about other piano players who also played on fish fries, songs, violences and stuff.

Oh. Well, Deku used to play. This boy used to play. Boynton El Centiocho used to play. Fish fries. Right. But he was an early piano player. He learned how to play piano early when he died young. He was thirty years old when he died. I know, baby, when he got dope, you know. Oh boy. Well, I don't even smoke a good cigarette. Yeah, brother.
Do you smoke bad cigarettes? Huh? Do you smoke bad cigarettes? Who? You said you don't smoke good cigarettes? I don't smoke no kind of cigarettes. Oh, I'm sorry. No.

No. I don't smoke no kind of cigarettes. Nothing, huh? Nothing. No. But I mean, brother said, yeah. This guy, yeah, he's still living. Walter Deku. You know him, man? Yeah. Well, he's still living. You know that? I didn't know that. Yeah, he's a wino. He drinks wine like that. I don't know. Walter Deku? Walter Deku? Walter Deku. Do you know how to find him? Huh? I wouldn't know. I don't know where he's in. I haven't seen him. I don't know. I used to play with him at the old folks home now when he was playing there. Lachington. Lachington. Yeah, he's playing there, you know. Yeah. And Chinese Charlie, well, he's a dead poor boy. That's all I know him. That's how he looked like the Chinaman, you know. The drama? No. No, not that Chinese. No, it's Chinese Charlie. Well, he died young, too. What did he play? Piano. He was a piano. He did also play all these fish fries. Huh? Yeah, he played a lot of fish fries. What? Chinese Charlie. Chinese Charlie. Do you know his real name? No, I don't know his real name. He used to gather, you know.
I don't know. I called him Chinese Charlie. That's all I know. He used to like tell the role of Mokin. Yeah.
Did he sing Chinese Charlie? No, he never sang. He played piano. He was a good piano player.
Did he have any crips? Huh? Did he have a real crip that he played or featured or anything?

What do you mean by a crip? One of his special numbers. Well, he was a good piano player. Yeah? Juby. I know Juby. He was a good piano player, too. Juby? Juby. Well, them fellas all come over 20, over 30 years ago, you know. Yeah. That's the fellas that I knew. Well, then when I was a young guy, too, you know. He was just coming up, playing. And I played in a lot of tongues. You know. And them, what you call it? Places where they, Forbidden to Sound of Laker. What you call it? Speakeasy. Speakeasy, yeah. Playing the gang of that. Speakeasy. Oh, man. Willie. Yeah. Had another piano player. Willie. Red Car U. You didn't know him, man. Never met him. Never met him. Never met him. Met him, but he was a good piano player. And, uh, Willie. He was a good piano player.
Oh, they had nothing but some good, you know. Which Willie is this? Willie? That's all I know.
How did he die? I don't know. Oh, they drank so much, man.
Yeah. Well, you know, Willie Clark, he got killed, uh, he went to the toilet on Mardi Gras, and they killed him, because he had a flash of money.
That's Red Car U. That's Red Car U? I met him. He went, he left here. He beat the woman. And he went to California. Wow. That's why you met him.
No, I didn't meet him. I just got this picture.

Oh, he looked like him. Well, he was a good guy. It looks like him? No. That was, he was a bright, he was, you call him, bright brickhead. Bad hair. Bad hair? Bad hair, yeah. Red hair? Red looking hair, yeah. But bad. You know what a brickhead is? Oh, yeah. Huh?
Yeah. A fella that's real bright and he's got red hair. Red looking, bad hair. Yeah. A Marani, uh, what, Marani? What are they called, the Maronis too? Did you ever hear of that?

Marani. Marani, I'm okay. Marani, brickhead, that's what it is. Marani? Marani brickhead. I was in Hot Springs and talking to a fella. He said, you from New Orleans? And I said, yeah. I said, what they call a brickhead? I said, well, pal, I really don't know. He was one. He was a typical brickhead. I didn't want to tell him he was one. You know, Marani brickhead. Because both of us was there taking his batch, you know? He was taking them and I was taking them. And I said, well, I really don't know what a brickhead is now. He's like me. I don't know nothing about a brickhead. But he was one. A typical, you know, a typical brickhead. Well, they called me Fan because I looked like a Chinaman when I was small.
Like Fan Tan? Yeah, like a Chinaman. You know, a fan. You know, them Chinamans like fans, you know?
Yeah. And I had blackhead, long, long blackhead. Well, everything had turned silver now.

Yeah. When your hair has turned silver. That's right. When your hair has turned silver. What were you doing in Hot Springs? You were taking the leg. Well, I had my money. I was making my money so much. Yeah. And you just went up there to take your money? That's right. I went up there twice.

They have plenty of support up there? Well, I could have got a job playing in a nightclub up there. I went and I touched that pen and said, you say, how long are you going to be here, Fred? I said, well, I'm just here for 21 days. I'm going back home. He said, why don't you stay here? You have a job playing at camp if you want. I said, I'm going back to my lottery. I was making an old 250 a week, you know? It was good money 20 years ago. 25, 30 years ago, you know? Did you ever go out to Chicago? Yeah, I stayed in Chicago 60 days. 60 days? 60 days, yeah. I left. See, Campbell the Forest. It started snowing that day and I left. I borrowed money. I spent all my little change I had and I borrowed money to come home.
What year was it? 1922. That's a good one, isn't it?
Did you play there up in Chicago or else? Yeah, well, I was living there at the piano.
Marnie Jones, you know him? Marnie Jones? You know him? Piano player? I know who you're talking about. That's John L's cousin. Well, I was playing the piano. He said, how are you going to be here?

I said, well, I don't know. He said, well, he was staying. Sell them blues. I said, well, I ain't staying here, pal. I'm going back home and writing my lottery. I was making nice money, you know what I mean? My mother was living. That was my father. His dad. My brother was living. My brother. My brother used to work for A.J. Formback. He was the head man. The head man for the game, you know? He had a lot of money. Take out the money. We had them big tables, you know? He didn't know the big dice tables, you know? They had them. Then I got on the road with Kuyper. You know Kuyper? Trump?
I heard of him. I know his top of his brother on the phone.

I got on the road with the type of things that's tough, you know? He was closing up when the district was open. You heard about the district, huh? Yeah. He was running when the district was open. No, no, no. When the district was open, I used to write a lot of y'all through the district. You know, I was used to play a lot of y'all. Plenty a lot of y'all. Well, then he closed the district down. He closed everything down. He got caught on those speakeasers, you know? So Kuyper comes and says, you want to take a little trip? I said, wait. He said, what's going on, rolling? He said, okay, I'll go. I'll wait. First place we hit the McCloughan Hotel in Cone, Mississippi. And we played that same night. He said, what's the name of this band? I said, what's y'all going to name your band, pal? New Orleans Harmony Kings. First we played in the drugstore. They had a piano there, up in the balcony, you know? Yeah? Yeah. So I said, man, get on the piano, start playing, we're going to pass the hat. I said, okay. So I got on the piano. Good piano, too. I got on the piano, too. So they had a band at the Plugin Hotel, and the boys heard the music and they came over. And I had Charlie Love playing trumpet, man. You know, Charlie Love was a good trumpet player. Oh, yeah? And I said, where y'all going? I said, well, we just come out of the Orleans and going on the road. He said, well, y'all playing at night? I said, we ain't playing nowhere. He said, y'all want to play tonight? I said, where? He said, right over there in the hotel, McCloughan Hotel.
I said, okay.

We went over there and we played that night. And we left there and the next day we played a matinee dance and we got on the road and started hustling. You know what I mean? Just take our instruments out at night, in the day, in the evening, like, and play a couple of numbers and say, we're playing somewhere tonight. And we'll hide the hall, you know, and go play there. So much to come in and make that little change every night.
How big was this band?
Huh?
How big? Five pieces, that's all. You had Kaipa? Yeah, Kaipa, me, and we had a Slime Tramble.

And we had the drummer. Just all we had, five pieces, I can't remember who was in the band, you know? You said Charlie Love was there too. Yeah, Charlie Love was there. Kaipa, no, no, Charlie Love wasn't. Willie Pajot. Oh. I was on the road with Willie Pajot and Charlie Love. Yeah, that was another time. That was another time, yeah. We went to Donison, not Donisonville. One of them little country towns there. We stayed at, on Narrow Street, the 16-hundred block. And we played a couple of jobs and I said, well otherwise, I think I'm going to know him. I said, this band ain't doing, this band ain't doing good. And then I was getting money from the, what you call it, people that I would work for. And I put in my, you know, to get some change. Like pension? Yeah, pension. You know, you'd get a pension. Get so much, maybe, so much every two weeks you get. Cause I got to go back home and write my, write, write my name on the book. So I can get my little pension.
Oh, unemployment.

Unemployment pension, yeah. Yeah. Well, you had to get some money somewhere. Then when the lodge opened up again, well, come back home. Then start working again, you know. She made money, I made money for sending that lodge. I had a shop at my house, I had a woman working with it for me, keeping her so much a week.
When you were in Chicago, did you have a regular job as solo piano player or what?
No, no, I just was playing at a, where I was stopping, they had a piano, and I just practiced on a piano every day, you know. Uh huh.
Did you meet any other New Orleans music piano players up in Chicago, except mine?
Well, no, no, I just met this fellow, Manny Jones. And I used to go and listen at, when I, book. You remember book? No.
You mean the cornet player?
Yeah. What block? He was playing at, in the 3300 block, State Street.
Is that near the Royal Gardens? No, the Royal Gardens, around? The Royal Gardens, around?
The Royal Gardens, around on, uh, 30th Street.
One-eyed buck?
One-eyed buck. You mean bad-eyed Joe? Joe? He's, he's the fellow that sent for the, that's Louis Armstrong. That'd be Joe Oliver.
Joe Oliver, that's his name. Yeah, yeah. One-eyed buck. One-eyed buck. I never heard a guy. I heard a bad-eyed Joe, but never one. One-eyed buck. Mm- dear
The final piece was most extreme. Second real of the band.

Then I had, I called it a banjo. One of the last I could get a guitar player, I called it a banjo player. Willie. Willie Van Teese. Oh yeah. Got him two banjos. Two banjos in your band. Yeah, two banjos. Sound good too. Willie had a good, real good banjo. Cause we was playing down on France Street. A fellow by the name of Jimmy Duport. But he couldn't get nobody in the place. Yeah, and she worked for Lulu? No, she was, even Lulu had girls working in there.

Yeah. All kinds. Yeah. Brooms, brunettes, and everything, you know? Anyone you want to pick. You know what I mean? Roseanne in that house, 26. I didn't even know how many brooms they had in there. Were you in all of them? No, all of them, no. I was in the kitchen. Where the food is. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
The 4th reel we got on now. A fan-virgin. You got some more questions in case you called?
Uh, yeah. Do I really? Did you know a cabaret called the alley? The alley? The alley. Cabaret? Just a drinking place. I don't know. There are so many places.
Well, that was around St. Bernard and the market, sort of behind the market.
The French market?
Behind the circle, the St. Bernard circle, right around in there. What's the name? The alley. Oh, yeah.
Cabaret? Alley. Alley, yeah. My brother used to work in the alley. You mean play or what? The deal money. You know what they call money? No, you don't know. Three card money.
Four card.
Four card?
Four card.
Yeah, that's where. Andre Dominguez. You ever heard of him?
Is he related to Paul?
Paul Dominguez?
Yeah.
Paul's brother. Yeah. You know Paul then? I know.

segments.chapter: Opening and who he played with
segments.title: Opening: date, address and finding old musicians
segments.summary: Interviewers confirm the date (13 September 1972) and an address, and Bourgeau talks about asking elderly relatives who might remember his father's era.

segments.chapter: Opening and who he played with
segments.title: Fred Washington and the musicians Bourgeau played with
segments.summary: Asked about pianist Fred Washington, then lists men he played with: Chris Kelly, Walter Pichon, Kid Howard and Kid Thomas.

segments.chapter: Opening and who he played with
segments.title: Johnny St. Cyr, Lawrence Tucker, Peter Williams and Blue
segments.summary: He recalls starting on guitar with Johnny St. Cyr and playing with Lawrence Tucker, Peter Williams and Blue, who drank himself to death.

segments.chapter: Opening and who he played with
segments.title: Piano job at the Oasis with Albert Francis and Hughes
segments.summary: He played piano nine to three nightly for about two years at a nightclub with a Dixieland band including Albert Francis on drums and a sax player named Hughes; also Pico and Peter Williams.

segments.chapter: Banjo, piano and his own bands
segments.title: Recording session with Kid Thomas and George's borrowed banjo
segments.summary: Asked about a recording session with Kid Thomas and George, he recalls little but tells how George borrowed his banjos and never returned one.

segments.chapter: Banjo, piano and his own bands
segments.title: Forming his own band with Harold Christophe and Leroy Thompson
segments.summary: He assembled his own band with Henry Ravallon, Clarence and Harold Christophe, later adding Leroy Thompson after Blue died.

segments.chapter: Banjo, piano and his own bands
segments.title: Getting his first banjo and learning to play
segments.summary: A fellow gave him a five-string banjo, he taught himself from a book, and soon bought and sold many banjos.

segments.chapter: Banjo, piano and his own bands
segments.title: Playing piano with Johnny St. Cyr on Airline Highway
segments.summary: He played piano on Friday and Saturday nights at the 4900 Airline Highway with St. Cyr on guitar about twenty years earlier; mentions his pension.

segments.chapter: Banjo, piano and his own bands
segments.title: Five-string banjo technique and tuning
segments.summary: He played with a pick, removed the fifth string, and tells of a jam session with a four-string-looking banjo.

segments.chapter: Banjo, piano and his own bands
segments.title: Learning piano, Bill Russell, the Banner Club and Burnell
segments.summary: Bill Russell asked about Jelly Roll Morton, whom he cooked Monday dinners for; he learned piano on a club piano, played the Banner Club with George, and praises pianist Burnell.

segments.chapter: Banjo, piano and his own bands
segments.title: Sam Hopkins, the Toyamas, Antoines and picnic jobs
segments.summary: Interviewers ask for contact details of Sam Hopkins, Lawrence Eddergren and the Japanese banjoist; he talks about drummers Paul and Harold Antoine and picnic work.

segments.chapter: Piano players, Hot Springs and Chicago
segments.title: Fish fries and early piano players: Deku, Chinese Charlie, Juby
segments.summary: Asked about back-alley fish fries, he names piano players Walter Deku, Chinese Charlie and Juby who played them.

segments.chapter: Piano players, Hot Springs and Chicago
segments.title: Speakeasies, Willie Red Car U, brickheads and the nickname Fan
segments.summary: He recalls speakeasy piano players, the pianist Willie, a talk about brickheads in Hot Springs, and how he got the name Fan.

segments.chapter: Piano players, Hot Springs and Chicago
segments.title: Gambling trips to Hot Springs and a stay in Chicago
segments.summary: He went to Hot Springs twice and stayed 60 days in Chicago, returning home to his lottery work paying good money.

segments.chapter: Piano players, Hot Springs and Chicago
segments.title: Brother's gambling job and the road with Kuyper's Harmony Kings
segments.summary: Playing piano in Chicago, then after the district closed he went on the road with Kuyper's New Orleans Harmony Kings, starting at a hotel in Mississippi.

segments.chapter: Piano players, Hot Springs and Chicago
segments.title: Hustling jobs on the road and the Willie Pajot trip
segments.summary: Their five-piece band took work night to night; another trip with Willie Pajot and Charlie Love failed, so he returned home for unemployment pay.

segments.chapter: Piano players, Hot Springs and Chicago
segments.title: Chicago piano playing and musicians he heard there
segments.summary: In Chicago he practiced piano where he stayed, heard Manny Jones and a cornetist on State Street, and discusses Joe Oliver and the Royal Gardens.

segments.chapter: On the road and later jobs
segments.title: Two banjos, Jimmy Duport's place and Harold Christophe's call
segments.summary: He recalls a band with two banjos including Willie, playing parties at Jimmy Duport's place, and his last job with Harold Christophe; his hands hurt.

segments.chapter: On the road and later jobs
segments.title: Records for Ken Mills and a trio with Sylvester Hand
segments.summary: He made records for Ken Mills and played as a trio with Sylvester Hand and a drummer, earning more than with the full band.

segments.chapter: Violinists, Jimmy Noon and Decatur Street
segments.title: Violinists: Peter Williams, Piron and Sam Morgan's band
segments.summary: Third reel begins with Sam Morgan, then violinists, including Piron, a reading jazz violinist who led a six-piece band at the lake.

segments.chapter: Violinists, Jimmy Noon and Decatur Street
segments.title: Peter Alexander and his son P.J.
segments.summary: Peter Alexander is dead and has a son in Baltimore called P.J.

segments.chapter: Violinists, Jimmy Noon and Decatur Street
segments.title: Jimmy Noon as a neighbour
segments.summary: Jimmy Noon lived next door about fifty years earlier and played clarinet and then saxophone.

segments.chapter: Violinists, Jimmy Noon and Decatur Street
segments.title: Playing the parlor and Decatur Street, ending at the Virginia Kitchen
segments.summary: He tells of a poorly paid job at the parlor, playing Decatur Street dives and ending each night at the Virginia Kitchen.

segments.chapter: Violinists, Jimmy Noon and Decatur Street
segments.title: Boots and Sport Young, and boogie-woogie in early bands
segments.summary: Interviewer names Sport and Boots Young; Bourgeau says early bands played boogie-woogie blues and Dixieland, with violin, piano, banjo and bass.

segments.chapter: Violinists, Jimmy Noon and Decatur Street
segments.title: Pico's four-piece band, George Jones and the horse sound
segments.summary: Back to Peter Alexander, his wife and clarinetist Pico in a four-piece band; George Jones on bass; a phone-call break and a question about the horse sound.

segments.chapter: Violinists, Jimmy Noon and Decatur Street
segments.title: Manuel's son and a phone call
segments.summary: Interviewer asks about Manuel's son who played cornet; Bourgeau remembers him; the interviewer makes a phone call.

segments.chapter: Army in France
segments.title: Army in France in World War I
segments.summary: He reached France after the war ended, was the only French speaker in his company of 250, and played boogie-woogie blues on an organ in a boxcar.

segments.chapter: Pianists, the district and Stormy Weather
segments.title: Cornet players D.D. and Billy and Blue's drinking
segments.summary: Talk about a cornetist and his work with D.D. and Billy, then Blue's drinking, and the number of jobs in his book.

segments.chapter: Pianists, the district and Stormy Weather
segments.title: Sheet music, a pianist who read music, and Dr. Blanks
segments.summary: Who has old sheet music; a piano player who couldn't play without music; his brother-in-law Dr. Herbert Blanks and a hard baby grand piano.

segments.chapter: Pianists, the district and Stormy Weather
segments.title: Piano technique, the district and Zeno's ballroom
segments.summary: Talk of black-key players, Ed Mercier, his visits to the district at age nine and playing piano at Zeno's ballroom.

segments.chapter: Pianists, the district and Stormy Weather
segments.title: Simon Trajan, Saeed and Joe Robichaud's father
segments.summary: After a tape pause: the Trajan brothers, Joe Robichaud and playing with his father's big band.

segments.chapter: Pianists, the district and Stormy Weather
segments.title: Pianists Wilson and Paul Louie, Newky Johnson and George Thomas
segments.summary: Asked about pianists, he discusses Newky Johnson, Willie Jackson, George Thomas and who wrote Big Buck Blues.

segments.chapter: Pianists, the district and Stormy Weather
segments.title: Stormy Weather, his habits and his family
segments.summary: He played with a pianist called Stormy Weather in the district, who drank heavily; the interviewers seek his sister.

segments.chapter: Pianists, the district and Stormy Weather
segments.title: Cooney, Lulu White and an actress in France
segments.summary: He cannot place Cooney, then recounts an actress in France asking about Lulu White of 235 Basin Street and his visits in the kitchen.

segments.chapter: Reel four
segments.title: Fourth reel: the Alley cabaret and Andre Dominguez
segments.summary: New reel begins; questions about the Alley cabaret where his brother dealt four-card money, and Andre Dominguez.
